newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: LIB BACKBENCHER SAYS 10 POINT PLAN MUST NOT BE DILUTED
A Liberal Party backbencher says he and his colleagues will be standing their ground on native title.
The Opposition says it's not happy with the Prime Minister's 10 point native title plan, and John Howard will meet Kim Beazley this week to try to reach an agreement on it.
But Warren Entsch says backbenchers have given enough concessions, and the plan must go forward in its current form.
Mr Entsch says the plan may be tidied up, but there's no room for tinkering with its central requirements.
Mr Beazley says the Opposition won't support the plan in its current form, even if that means forcing a double dissolution election.
CREATIONIST WAS WRONG, BUT ENDS UP IN THE RIGHT
The Federal Court has concluded that church minister, Doctor Alan Roberts, falsely claimed he was involved in the search for Noah's Ark, in Turkey.
This is despite his legal victory in a case brought by Melbourne scientist, Professor Ian Plimer.
The Court today dismissed Professor Plimer's legal action against creationist and minister, Doctor Roberts, on a technicality.

However, in delivering his judgement, Justice Ronald Sackville said the doctor falsely claimed in a series of lectures in 1992 that he personally carried out tests on the rock formation in the Middle East.
Outside the court, Doctor Roberts said he's delighted at the dismissal of the case.
ACCC REPORT INTO POSSIBLE BANK COLLUSION OUT TODAY
The results of an investigation into possible collusion between the major banks in setting home loan interest rates is expected to be handed to the Federal Treasurer this afternoon.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission launched the inquiry after the four major banks dropped their rates by exactly the same amount, in response to the Reserve Bank official rate cut ten days ago.
All the big four banks initially refused pass on the full half of one percent cut in official interest rates, reducing them by just 0.35 percent.
However, early last week the ANZ bank passed on the full half a percent cut, by dropping its variable home loan rate by a further 0.15 percent.
DELAY IN EXAMINATION OF CEMETERY SELL-OFF
A committee appointed to look at the proposed privatisation of cemeteries in Victoria is not expected to report back on its findings until September.
It was hoped the committee would report back to Health Minister, Rob Knowles, this month, but a spokesperson says there've been more submissions than expected.
The State Government has been looking at privatisation after being lobbied by two large funeral companies.
BEAZLEY: GOVT BREAKING A PROMISE TO MINING INDUSTRY
The Federal Opposition says plans to cap the mining industry's diesel fuel rebate breach a promise the Government made to the industry last year.
The Government has written to the Minerals Council saying it wants to cap the rebate at $813 million, the amount allocated to it in the Budget.
Opposition leader, Kim Beazley, says the plan would devastate the industry, threatening its recent strong growth.
Mr Beazley says Western Australia would be hardest hit by the change because it has a lot of small operators.
PLAN TO CAP MINING INDUSTRY DIESEL REBATE MAY BE UNPOPULAR

The Federal Government looks like facing a battle to implement plans to cap the mining industry's diesel fuel rebate. Finance Minister John Fahey has written to the Minerals Council of Australia, saying the Government wants to wind back rebate payments if they exceed $813 million.
But Liberal backbencher, Wilson Tuckey, says any increase in the cost of mining makes it less profitable to mine lesser grades of ore.
Mr Tuckey says the plan has not been approved by the party room or the Government's Primary Industries Committee, of which he is a member.
Mr Fahey and two other Ministers will meet mining industry leaders later this month to discuss the proposal.
ABORIGINES URGED TO COMPLAIN ABOUT HUMAN RIGHTS ABUSES
A former Director of the Foreign Affairs Human Rights section says the Federal Government is probably in violation of many international human rights standards.
Bill Barker is holding a series of seminars around Australia to encourage indigenous people to complain to the United Nations about human rights violations by the Government.
Mr Barker says Aboriginal people should become active in UN forums.
He says the government is probably in violation of a number of standards it has signed, including the Genocide Convention in relation to indigenous children forcibly taken from their families.
Mr Barker says successive Australian governments have endorsed UN human rights conventions and should expect them to be used.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
